Modern controllers and devices have motors built‑in to provide haptic feedback. Adding rumbles and vibrations can provide subtle feedback that is hard to convey through visuals or audio.

Roblox supports haptics for the following devices:

  • Android and iOS phones supporting haptics including most iPhone, Pixel, and Samsung Galaxy devices
  • PlayStation gamepads

class/HapticService.d:
HapticService allows scripts to query vibration support and set motor intensities on gamepad controllers, VR controllers, and mobile devices. Use IsVibrationSupported() and IsMotorSupported() to check device capabilities, then SetMotor() to drive a specific VibrationMotor on a given UserInputType. Motor output is scaled by the user's haptic intensity preference in their Roblox settings.

As this service is client-side only, it can only be used in a LocalScript, a ModuleScript required by a LocalScript, or a Script with RunContext set to RunContext.Client.

This service has been superseded by HapticEffect, which supports waveform-based effects, looping, spatial attenuation, and preset effect types. For new work, use HapticEffect instead.

class/HeapProfilerService.d:
HeapProfilerService captures snapshots of the Luau heap so that memory-profiling tools can analyze script memory usage. Requesting a profile runs a full garbage-collection cycle and then walks the heap of the target Luau virtual machine, producing a JSON report that breaks memory down by value type, memory category, and userdata class, together with an aggregated ownership graph and a list of unique and unparented instance references.

Profiles can be requested for either the server or a specific client. HeapProfilerService:ServerRequestDataAsync() returns the server's profile and HeapProfilerService:ClientRequestDataAsync() returns a given player's client profile. When the profiled machine differs from the caller, the data is generated remotely, compressed, and replicated back through the HeapProfilerService.OnNewData event before the yielding call resolves.
class/HeapProfilerService.s: Generates and retrieves Luau heap memory profiles from the client and server Luau virtual machines for memory debugging.

m.d:
Requests a Luau heap profile from the client belonging to player. When called on that client itself, the profile is generated locally and returned immediately. When called from the server, a request is sent to the client and this function yields until the compressed profile is replicated back through HeapProfilerService.OnNewData, decompressed, and returned. If the client does not respond within 10 seconds, the request fails.

The returned string is JSON containing a Report section (heap memory broken down by value type, memory category, and userdata class, plus an aggregated size graph) and a Refs section (unique and unparented instance references).
m.s: Yields until the Luau heap profile of the specified player's client is available, then returns it as a JSON string.

p.s: The Player whose client Luau heap should be profiled.

r.s: A JSON-encoded string containing the client's Luau heap profile.

m.d:
Requests a Luau heap profile from the server. When called on the server, the profile is generated locally and returned immediately. When called from a client, a request is sent to the server and this function yields until the compressed profile is replicated back through HeapProfilerService.OnNewData, decompressed, and returned. If the server does not respond within 10 seconds, the request fails.

The returned string has the same JSON structure as HeapProfilerService:ClientRequestDataAsync().
m.s: Yields until the server's Luau heap profile is available, then returns it as a JSON string.

r.s: A JSON-encoded string containing the server's Luau heap profile.

m.d: Delivers a Luau heap profile that was generated on a remote machine in response to a HeapProfilerService:ClientRequestDataAsync() or HeapProfilerService:ServerRequestDataAsync() call. The profile JSON is zstd-compressed and carried in jsonString; the receiving service decompresses it, matches it to the pending request by id, and resolves the yielding call. The compressedLength and uncompressedLength arguments report the buffer's size before and after decompression.
m.s: Fires on the requesting machine with the compressed Luau heap profile produced for an earlier request.

p.s: The Player the profile is being delivered to, or nil when the data is replicated to the server.
A buffer holding the zstd-compressed JSON heap profile.
The identifier of the request this data corresponds to.
The size, in bytes, of the compressed profile buffer.
The size, in bytes, of the heap profile JSON after decompression.

class/HiddenSurfaceRemovalAsset.d:
Engine-managed asset; its data is not exposed to scripts. Holds the hidden surface removal (HSR) data produced by Roblox's layered-clothing deformation pipeline. HSR identifies the faces of a wrap's mesh that are fully occluded by clothing layers worn above it, so the engine can strip those faces from the output geometry before rendering rather than drawing surfaces that will never be visible.

The asset is stored and fetched by content ID: the engine deserializes it and decodes its data into the runtime visibility information consumed by the wrap deformer when solving a WrapLayer or WrapTarget.
class/HiddenSurfaceRemovalAsset.s: Stores the precomputed hidden surface removal (HSR) data for a layered-clothing wrap, marking the mesh faces that are hidden by higher clothing layers so the engine can cull them.

class/Highlight.d:
The Highlight instance is a visual effect which you can use to call attention to a specific object within an experience. Every highlight effect has a silhouette outline that surrounds the object and a solid overlay interior that displays over the object. You can customize both of these components independently to modify the highlight's visual appearance.

Useful applications of the highlight effect include:

  • Providing visual feedback that an object is important and/or interactable.
  • Making distant objects visible through objects that are closer to the user.
  • Indicating the current position and status of other characters.

Limitations

As a performance limit, Studio only displays 255 simultaneous Highlight instances on the client at a time. If you exceed this limit, the additional instances are silently ignored. Note that while a Highlight with Enabled set to false doesn't display, it still takes one of the 255 available slots, so if you plan to permanently disable a Highlight instance, it's best to delete it rather than disable it.
class/Highlight.s: A visual effect which you can use to call attention to a specific object within an experience.

m.d: The Instance for which to apply the Highlight, used to apply the effect to an Instance outside of a child/parent relationship.
m.s: The `Class.Instance` that the `Class.Highlight` is applied to.

kid.simple: The object to highlight, if the Highlight is not inside it. If Adornee is empty, the Highlight highlights its parent.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local highlight = Instance.new("Highlight")
highlight.Adornee = Workspace:WaitForChild("Target")
highlight.Parent = Workspace

m.d:
Controls how the Highlight effect displays with respect to other objects in the world. You can set this property to one of the following options:

  • AlwaysOnTop — Allows the highlight to display regardless if there are objects between the camera and the highlighted object. This means the viewer is always able to see the highlight regardless of what is between the highlighted object and the camera.

  • Occluded — Hides the highlight if there are objects between the camera and the highlighted object. This means the viewer is only able to see the object if there are no obstructing objects between the highlighted object and the camera's view.
m.s: Controls how the `Class.Highlight` effect displays with respect to other objects in the world.

kid.simple: AlwaysOnTop means the highlight is visible even through walls. Occluded means it hides when something is in front of the object.
kid.example:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")
local highlight = Workspace:WaitForChild("Chest"):WaitForChild("Highlight")
highlight.DepthMode = Enum.HighlightDepthMode.Occluded

kid.simple: A Highlight makes an object stand out with a glowing outline and a colored fill over it. Put it inside a part, model, or character and that thing gets highlighted. It can even show through walls, which is great for showing teammates or important items.
kid.analogy: A Highlight is like running a highlighter marker around a picture in a book. The outline makes it pop out, and the fill colors it in, so your eye goes straight to it.

Show teammates or a target through walls.
Make a selected item glow while the player is choosing it.
kid.where: Put it inside the thing you want highlighted (a part, model, or character), or set its Adornee to point at that thing. Works in Scripts (everyone sees it) and LocalScripts (only that player sees it).

terms.fill / interior: The see-through color laid over the whole object.
terms.transparency: How see-through something is, from 0 (solid) to 1 (invisible).
terms.adornee: The object a Highlight decorates when it is not inside that object.

examples.title: Highlight a chest when the player gets close
examples.place: LocalScript in StarterPlayerScripts (with a Model named Chest in Workspace)
examples.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")

local player = Players.LocalPlayer
local chest = Workspace:WaitForChild("Chest")

local highlight = Instance.new("Highlight")
highlight.FillColor = Color3.fromRGB(255, 215, 0)  -- gold fill
highlight.OutlineColor = Color3.fromRGB(255, 255, 255) -- white outline
highlight.FillTransparency = 0.6
highlight.Enabled = false
highlight.Parent = chest

while true do
	local character = player.Character
	local root = character and character:FindFirstChild("HumanoidRootPart")
	if root then
		local distance = (root.Position - chest:GetPivot().Position).Magnitude
		highlight.Enabled = distance < 20 -- glow within 20 studs
	end
	task.wait(0.2)
end
explain: We make a gold Highlight inside the chest but start with it turned off.
Every 0.2 seconds we measure how far the player's character is from the chest (`.Magnitude` is the length of the gap, in studs).
If the player is closer than 20 studs, the highlight turns on. Because this is a LocalScript, only this player sees it.

gotchas: Only 255 Highlights can show at once on a player's screen; extras are ignored. Disabled Highlights still count, so Destroy ones you no longer need.
By default the highlight shows through walls (AlwaysOnTop). Set DepthMode to Occluded if it should hide behind walls.

class/HingeConstraint.d:
A HingeConstraint allows two Attachments to rotate about one axis, constraining the two Attachments so that they both occupy the same position and that their X axes point in the same direction.

Note that if this constraint attaches one part (A) to another part (B) that is anchored or connected to an anchored part (Z), part A will not be locally simulated when interacting with a player.

When configuring this constraint, it may be helpful to study Roblox Units to understand how Roblox units compare to metric units.

Angular Power

Hinges can be configured to actuate rotation. If a hinge's ActuatorType is set to Motor, it attempts to rotate the attachments with the goal of reaching its AngularVelocity. You can further control this rotation through both MotorMaxAcceleration and MotorMaxTorque. If a hinge's ActuatorType is set to Servo, it attempts to rotate to an angle specified by TargetAngle. This rotation is controlled by both AngularSpeed and ServoMaxTorque.

Limits

You can set limits to restrict the rotation of a hinge, useful for mechanisms like doors which should only swing open or closed within a set range. Enabling the LimitsEnabled property exposes the LowerAngle and UpperAngle limits, as well as Restitution which defines the elasticity of the attachments when they reach either limit.
class/HingeConstraint.s: Constrains its attachments to rotate about a single axis.

m.d:
Sets whether the rotation of the HingeConstraint is actuated and, if so, what kind of actuation.

  • If ActuatorType is set to Motor, the hinge will attempt to rotate the attachments with the goal of reaching AngularVelocity. This rotation is limited by both MotorMaxAcceleration and MotorMaxTorque.
  • If ActuatorType is set to Servo, the hinge will attempt to rotate to an angle specified by TargetAngle. This rotation is limited by both AngularSpeed and ServoMaxTorque.

Note that both actuated and free spinning rotation can be limited by setting LimitsEnabled to true.
m.s: Sets whether the rotation of the `Class.HingeConstraint` is actuated and, if so, what kind of actuation it uses.

kid.simple: Picks how the hinge is powered: None (free, just swings), Motor (keeps spinning at AngularVelocity) or Servo (turns to TargetAngle and holds).

m.d: This property specifies the sharpness of the servo motor in reaching the TargetAngle, when ActuatorType is set to Servo. Larger values correspond to a faster response and smaller values results in more damping and a slower response.
m.s: Specifies the sharpness of the servo motor in reaching the `Class.HingeConstraint.TargetAngle|TargetAngle`.

kid.simple: In Servo mode, how sharply it snaps to TargetAngle. Bigger numbers react faster; smaller numbers are softer and slower.

m.s: The desired angular speed a `Class.HingeConstraint` with `Class.HingeConstraint.ActuatorType|ActuatorType` set to `Enum.ActuatorType|Servo` will attempt to maintain while rotating towards its `Class.HingeConstraint.TargetAngle|TargetAngle`. Measured in radians/second.

print("Gate is open", hinge.CurrentAngle, "degrees")

If the Attachment reach the end of the limited range of rotation then they will stop rotating. kid.simple: If true, the hinge can only turn between LowerAngle and UpperAngle. It stops at the ends (and bounces if Restitution is above 0).

HingeConstraint lets two parts spin around one line, like a door on its hinges or a wheel on an axle. The two attachments stay on the same spot, and their X arrows (the hinge line) stay lined up. You can leave it free-spinning, power it like a motor, or make it turn to an exact angle like a servo.
kid.analogy: HingeConstraint is exactly like a door hinge or a wheel's axle: it can only swing or spin one way, around one line.
whenToUse: Doors and gates that swing
Car and cart wheels (Motor)
Drawbridges, levers and flippers (Servo)
Spinning windmills and fans
kid.where: Make it with Instance.new("HingeConstraint"), set Attachment0 and Attachment1 (one in each part), and put it in workspace. The hinge line is each attachment's X arrow, so turn the attachments so their X points along the axle.

terms.constraint: An invisible rule or connector that the physics engine follows, like 'these two parts must stay stuck together' or 'push this part upward'.
terms.attachment: A tiny invisible point you put inside a part. It has a position AND a direction (its own X, Y and Z arrows). Constraints grab parts by their attachments.
terms.Attachment0 / Attachment1: The two attachments a constraint connects. Attachment0 is usually the one that gets pushed or moved; Attachment1 is the other end or the goal.
terms.axis: An imaginary line something turns around or slides along. An attachment's X axis is its main arrow.
terms.anchored: An anchored part is frozen in place. Physics and constraint forces cannot move it. Set `part.Anchored = false` if you want a constraint to move it.
terms.unanchored: A part that physics is allowed to move. Constraints that push or pull only work on unanchored parts.
terms.torque: A twisting push that makes things spin, like turning a doorknob or a steering wheel. Torque = force x distance from the spinning point, so pushing farther from the center twists harder.
terms.angular velocity: How fast something spins, and around which axis, measured in radians per second. 2 x pi (about 6.28) radians per second is one full turn every second.
terms.radians: Another way to measure angles. A full circle is 2 x pi (about 6.28) radians, which is 360 degrees. `math.rad(90)` turns 90 degrees into radians.
terms.restitution: Bounciness, from 0 (no bounce, just stops) to 1 (bounces back as hard as it hit).
terms.actuator: The part of a constraint that powers movement by itself, like a motor. ActuatorType picks None (no power), Motor (keep spinning/moving at a speed) or Servo (move to a target spot and stop).
terms.motor (ActuatorType): Keeps turning or sliding at a set speed, like a fan or a car wheel.
terms.servo (ActuatorType): Moves to a set target angle or position and holds there, like a robot arm or an automatic door.
terms.limits: Stops that keep a joint from moving too far, like a door that can only swing 90 degrees.
terms.acceleration: How fast speed changes. The rule is F = m x a (force = mass x acceleration). Push a mass-5.6 part with force 56 and it speeds up by 10 studs/s every second.
terms.degrees: The usual way to measure angles: 90 degrees is a quarter turn, 360 is a full turn. TargetAngle, LowerAngle and UpperAngle use degrees.
terms.local simulation: When a player's own device is allowed to calculate a part's physics so it feels smooth. Parts hinged to anchored parts do not get this when players touch them, so they may feel a little delayed.

examples.title: A door that swings open to 90 degrees
examples.code:
local frame = workspace:WaitForChild("DoorFrame") -- anchored
local door = workspace:WaitForChild("Door")       -- unanchored

-- Both attachments at the door's edge. Rotate them so X points straight up (the hinge line).
local edge = door.CFrame * CFrame.new(-door.Size.X / 2, 0, 0)
local a0 = Instance.new("Attachment")
a0.Parent = frame
a0.WorldCFrame = edge * CFrame.Angles(0, 0, math.rad(90))
local a1 = Instance.new("Attachment")
a1.Parent = door
a1.WorldCFrame = a0.WorldCFrame

local hinge = Instance.new("HingeConstraint")
hinge.Attachment0 = a0
hinge.Attachment1 = a1
hinge.ActuatorType = Enum.ActuatorType.Servo
hinge.ServoMaxTorque = 100000 -- strong enough to swing the door
hinge.AngularSpeed = 2        -- radians per second while moving
hinge.TargetAngle = 0         -- closed
hinge.Parent = frame

task.wait(2)
hinge.TargetAngle = 90 -- swing open a quarter turn
explain: Both attachments sit at the door's left edge. Rotating them 90 degrees around Z makes their X arrow point straight up, so the hinge line is vertical, like a real door.
Servo mode means 'turn to TargetAngle and hold there'. TargetAngle is in degrees.
AngularSpeed (about 2 radians per second, roughly 115 degrees per second) is how fast it swings.
ServoMaxTorque must be big enough to move the door's weight.

examples.title: A motor wheel that keeps spinning
examples.code:
local hinge = workspace:WaitForChild("Cart"):WaitForChild("WheelHinge")

hinge.ActuatorType = Enum.ActuatorType.Motor
hinge.AngularVelocity = 10      -- target spin: 10 radians/s (about 1.6 turns per second)
hinge.MotorMaxTorque = 50000    -- how hard the motor can twist
hinge.MotorMaxAcceleration = math.huge -- reach that speed as fast as possible
explain: Motor mode spins the hinge at AngularVelocity, measured in radians per second. 2 x pi (6.28) is one turn per second.
MotorMaxTorque limits how hard it can twist. A heavy cart needs more.
A negative AngularVelocity spins the other way (drive backwards).

gotchas: The hinge spins around the attachments' X arrows. If your door spins the wrong way (like flipping over), rotate the attachments.
AngularVelocity and AngularSpeed are in radians per second, but TargetAngle, LowerAngle and UpperAngle are in degrees. Mixing these up is very common.
If the motor or servo does nothing, the max torque is probably too small.
If a part is hinged to an anchored part, physics for it is not calculated on the player's device, so it may feel slightly laggy to touch.

class/HttpService.d:
HttpService allows HTTP requests to be sent from experience servers using RequestAsync, GetAsync and PostAsync. This service allows experiences to be integrated with third-party web services such as analytics, data storage, remote server configuration, error reporting, advanced calculations, or real-time communication. Additionally, it can call a subset of the Open Cloud APIs.

For more information about these use cases, see In-experience HTTP requests.

HttpService also houses the JSONEncode and JSONDecode methods, which are useful for communicating with services that use the JSON format. In addition, the GenerateGUID method provides random 128‑bit labels which can be treated as probabilistically unique in a variety of scenarios.

Within Studio, use CreateWebStreamClient() to process data in real time from servers that support streaming protocols such as SSE, chunked transfer encoding, and WebSockets. You can connect callback functions to stream events, allowing you to process data immediately as it arrives instead of waiting for the entire response to complete.

Only send HTTP requests to trusted third-party platforms to avoid introducing unnecessary security risks to your experience.
class/HttpService.s: Allows sending HTTP requests and provides various web-related and JSON methods.

m.d:
When set to true, allows scripts to send requests to websites using HttpService:GetAsync(), HttpService:PostAsync(), and HttpService:RequestAsync().

This property must be toggled on for unpublished experiences by setting this property to true using the Command Bar:

game:GetService("HttpService").HttpEnabled = true
m.s: Indicates whether HTTP requests can be sent to external websites.

kid.simple: True if the game is allowed to send web requests. You normally switch it on in Game Settings > Security; scripts can read it but a normal script cannot change it.
kid.example:
-- Script in ServerScriptService
local HttpService = game:GetService("HttpService")

if not HttpService.HttpEnabled then
	warn("Turn on Allow HTTP Requests in Game Settings > Security")
end
kid.gotcha: JSON and GUID functions work even when this is false.

m.d:
This method creates a client that establishes a long-lived connection to servers utilizing various streaming technologies, such as Server-Sent Events (SSE). After the connection is established, the client fires signals that you can connect callback functions to with RBXScriptConnection. Use these callbacks to process messages as soon as they arrive, as well as respond to open, close, and error events.

There is a limit of four total clients allowed at one time. Close streams that you no longer need with WebStreamClient:Close(). When the stream is no longer needed, you should disconnect any associated RBXScriptConnections to avoid memory leaks.

This method is available in Studio only. If you use it inside scripts, make sure to remove any references before publishing the experience. We encourage you to create plugins with this feature for reusability and ease of use.
m.s: Creates a client that opens a persistent connection to stream data.

p.s: The type of streaming connection to intiialize the client with.
A dictionary containing information to be requested from the server. It is identical to requestOptions in HttpService:RequestAsync().

kid.simple: Opens a long-lasting connection to a website that sends data bit by bit (a stream), so you can handle each piece the moment it arrives. It only works in Studio, mostly for plugins and tools.
kid.gotcha: Only 4 can be open at once. Close them with `:Close()` and disconnect your connections when done. Remove this code before publishing.

m.d:
This method generates a random universally unique identifier (UUID) string. The sixteen octets of a UUID are represented as 32 hexadecimal (base 16) digits, displayed in five groups separated by hyphens in the form 8-4-4-4-12 for a total of 36 characters, for example 123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426655440000.

The UUID specification used is Version 4 (random), variant 1 (DCE 1.1, ISO/IEC 11578:1996). UUIDs of this version are the most commonly used due to their simplicity, as they are entirely randomly generated. Note that this version does not have certain features that other UUID versions have, such as encoded timestamps, MAC addresses, or time-based sorting like UUIDv7 or ULID.

There are over 5.3×1036 unique v4 UUIDs, in which the probability of finding a duplicate within 103 trillion UUIDs is one in a billion.

The wrapInCurlyBraces argument determines whether the returned string is wrapped in curly braces ({}). For instance:

  • true: {94b717b2-d54f-4340-a504-bd809ef5bf5c}
  • false: db454790-7563-44ed-ab4b-397ff5df737b

This method can be used regardless of whether HTTP requests are enabled.
m.s: Generates a UUID/GUID random string, optionally with curly braces.

p.s: Whether the returned string should be wrapped in curly braces ({}).

r.s: The randomly generated UUID.

kid.simple: Makes a random unique ID string. Pass `false` if you do not want curly braces around it. Works on server and client, even with HTTP turned off.
kid.example:
-- Script or LocalScript
local HttpService = game:GetService("HttpService")

print(HttpService:GenerateGUID())      --> {94b717b2-d54f-4340-a504-bd809ef5bf5c}
print(HttpService:GenerateGUID(false)) --> db454790-7563-44ed-ab4b-397ff5df737b

The url parameter also accepts a Secret value; use GetSecret combined with AddPrefix and AddSuffix to safely embed secret credentials (such as API keys) directly in the URL without exposing their values.

The returned Secret can be transformed using built-in methods such as Secret:AddPrefix(). It is expected to be sent as a part of an HTTP request.

For more information, see the usage guide.

kid.simple: Gets a secret (like an API key) that you stored in your game's settings on the Creator Hub. You can send it in a web request, but you cannot print it, so it stays hidden.
kid.example:
-- Script in ServerScriptService
local HttpService = game:GetService("HttpService")

local ok, secret = pcall(function()
	return HttpService:GetSecret("weather_api_key")
end)
if ok then
	-- Build a URL with the key hidden inside
	local url = secret:AddPrefix("https://api.example.com/weather?key=")
	pcall(function()
		print(HttpService:GetAsync(url))
	end)
end

m.d:
This method transforms a JSON object or array into a Luau table with the following characteristics:

  • Keys of the table are strings or numbers but not both. If a JSON object contains both, string keys are ignored.
  • An empty JSON object generates an empty Luau table ({}).
  • If the input string is not a valid JSON object, this method will throw an error.

To encode a Luau table into a JSON object, use the HttpService:JSONEncode() method.

This method can be used regardless of whether HTTP requests are enabled.
m.s: Decodes a JSON string into a Luau table.

p.s: The JSON object being decoded.

r.s: The decoded JSON object as a Luau table.

kid.simple: Turns JSON text into a Luau table. Errors if the text is not valid JSON, so use pcall if the text comes from outside.
kid.example:
-- Script or LocalScript
local HttpService = game:GetService("HttpService")

local data = HttpService:JSONDecode('{"name":"Ava","level":7}')
print(data.name, data.level) --> Ava 7

m.d:
This method transforms a Luau table into a JSON object or array based on the following guidelines:

  • Keys of the table must be either strings or numbers. If a table contains both, an array takes priority (string keys are ignored).
  • An empty Luau table ({}) generates an empty JSON array (e.g. []).
  • Whether passing a dictionary table or a numerically indexed table, avoid nil values for any index.
  • Cyclic table references cause an error.

This method allows values such as inf and nan which are not valid JSON. This may cause problems if you want to use the outputted JSON elsewhere.

This method also accepts buffers up to 50 MiB, which it encodes to base64 (and often compresses) before converting to a JSON object.

To reverse the encoding process and decode a JSON object, use the HttpService:JSONDecode() method.

This method can be used regardless of whether HTTP requests are enabled.
m.s: Generate a JSON string from a Luau table.

p.s: The input Luau table.

r.s: The returned JSON string.

kid.simple: Turns a Luau table into JSON text, ready to send to a website or store as text.
kid.example:
-- Script or LocalScript
local HttpService = game:GetService("HttpService")

local text = HttpService:JSONEncode({ name = "Ava", level = 7 })
print(text) --> {"name":"Ava","level":7} (order may differ)
kid.gotcha: Things like Parts, Vector3 or functions cannot be turned into JSON. Use plain numbers, strings, booleans and tables.

It functions similarly to RequestAsync() except that it accepts HTTP request parameters as method parameters instead of a single dictionary and returns only the body of the HTTP response. Generally, this method is useful only as a shorthand and RequestAsync() should be used in most cases.

When true, the compress parameter controls whether a large request body is compressed using gzip.

The url parameter also accepts a Secret value — use GetSecret combined with AddPrefix and AddSuffixto safely embed secret credentials (such as API keys) directly in the URL without exposing their values.

Determines whether the data is compressed (gzipped) when sent.

kid.simple: Server only. Sends data to a web address with a POST request and returns the reply text. The data is usually JSON text.

-- Script in ServerScriptService
local HttpService = game:GetService("HttpService")

local body = HttpService:JSONEncode({ event = "PlayerWon", score = 99 })

m.d:
This method sends an HTTP request using a dictionary to specify the request data, such as the target URL, method, headers, and request body data. It returns a dictionary that describes the response data received. Optionally, the request can be compressed using HttpCompression.

Request dictionary fields
Name Type Required Description
Url String yes The target URL for this request. Must use http or https protocols.
Method String no The HTTP method being used by this request, most often GET or POST.
Headers Dictionary no A dictionary of headers to be used with this request. Most HTTP headers are accepted here, but not all.
Body String no The request body. Can be any string, including binary data. Must be excluded when using the GET or HEAD HTTP methods. It might be necessary to specify the Content-Type header when sending JSON or other formats.
Compress Enum.HttpCompression no An optional compression field that will compress the data in the request. The value can either be Enum.HttpCompression.None or Enum.HttpCompression.Gzip.
Timeout Integer no An optional timeout value in seconds to make requests time out more quickly. Values must be greater than zero and no greater than the default request timeout. This can be useful when debugging hanging requests.
Supported HTTP methods

The HTTP request methods specify the purpose of the request being made and what is expected if the request is successful. For instance, the GET request method tells the server at the requested address that a resource is being requested and, if it succeeds, the resource at that address will be returned. Similarly, the HEAD request method does the same except the server knows to return a response without a Body element.

Method Description Safe
GET  ⓘ The GET method requests the resource at the specified address. Does not support use of the Body parameter. Yes
HEAD  ⓘ The HEAD method requests a response identical to a GET request, but with no response body. Does not support use of the Body parameter. Yes
POST  ⓘ The POST method submits the supplied Body data to the requested address. No
PUT  ⓘ The PUT method replaces all current iterations of the resource specified within the supplied Body data. No
DELETE  ⓘ The DELETE method deletes the resource specified in the supplied Body data at the requested address. No
OPTIONS  ⓘ The OPTIONS method requests the permitted communication options for the supplied address. Yes
TRACE  ⓘ The TRACE method performs a message loop-back test along the path to the resource specified in the supplied Body data. Yes
PATCH  ⓘ The PATCH method applies partial changes to the resource specified in the supplied Body data at the requested address. No
HTTP headers

In the request dictionary, you can specify custom HTTP headers to use in the request. However, some headers cannot be specified. For example, Content-Length is determined from the request body. User-Agent and Roblox-Id are locked by Roblox. Other headers like Accept or Cache-Control use default values but can be overridden. More commonly, some REST APIs may require API keys or other service authentication to be specified in request headers.

The RequestAsync() method does not detect the format of body content. Many web servers require the Content-Type header be set appropriately when sending certain formats. Other methods of HttpService use the HttpContentType enum; for this method set the Content-Type header appropriately: text/plain, text/xml, application/xml, application/json or application/x-www-form-urlencoded are replacement Content-Type header values for the respective enum values.

Response dictionary fields

RequestAsync() returns a dictionary containing the following fields:

Name Type Description
Success Boolean The success status of the request. This is true if and only if the StatusCode lies within the range 200-299.
StatusCode Integer The HTTP response code identifying the status of the response.
StatusMessage String The status message that was sent back.
Headers Dictionary A dictionary of headers that were set in this response.
Body The request body (content) received in the response.
Error Cases

RequestAsync() raises an error if the response times out or if the target server rejects the request. If a web service goes down for some reason, it can cause scripts that use this method to stop functioning altogether. It is often a good idea to wrap calls to this method in LuaGlobals.pcall() and gracefully handle failure cases if the required information isn't available.

Limitations

The current limitation for sending and receiving external HTTP requests is 500 requests per minute. There is also a separate limit of 2500 requests per minute for Open Cloud requests. Requests over these thresholds will fail.
m.s: Sends an HTTP request using any HTTP method given a dictionary of information.

p.s: A dictionary containing information to be requested from the server specified.

r.s: A dictionary containing response information from the server specified.

kid.simple: Server only. The most flexible web request. You give a table with `Url`, and optionally `Method` (like "GET" or "POST"), `Headers` and `Body`. You get back a table with `Success`, `StatusCode`, `StatusMessage`, `Headers` and `Body`.
kid.example:
-- Script in ServerScriptService
local HttpService = game:GetService("HttpService")

local ok, response = pcall(function()
	return HttpService:RequestAsync({
		Url = "https://httpbin.org/post",
		Method = "POST",
		Headers = { ["Content-Type"] = "application/json" },
		Body = HttpService:JSONEncode({ hello = "world" }),
	})
end)

if ok and response.Success then
	print("Status:", response.StatusCode) --> 200
else
	warn("Request failed")
end

m.d:
This method percent-encodes a given string so that reserved characters properly encoded with % and two hexadecimal characters.

This is useful when formatting URLs for use with HttpService:GetAsync()/HttpService:PostAsync(), or POST data of the media type application/x-www-form-urlencoded (Enum.HttpContentType.ApplicationUrlEncoded).

For instance, when you encode the URL https://www.roblox.com/discover#/, this method returns https%3A%2F%2Fwww%2Eroblox%2Ecom%2Fdiscover%23%2F.
m.s: Replaces URL-unsafe characters with '%' and two hexadecimal characters.

p.s: The string (URL) to encode.

r.s: The encoded string.

kid.simple: Makes text safe to put inside a web address by replacing spaces and special characters with % codes. For example, a space becomes `%20`.
kid.example:
-- Script or LocalScript
local HttpService = game:GetService("HttpService")

local safe = HttpService:UrlEncode("cats & dogs")
print(safe) --> cats%20%26%20dogs

kid.simple: HttpService lets your game's server talk to websites outside of Roblox, like a weather site or your own web server. It also has handy tools that work anywhere: turning tables into JSON text and back, and making random unique IDs.
kid.analogy: HttpService is like the server's phone line to the outside world. Players' devices cannot use this phone; only the server can make calls, and only after you switch the phone on in Game Settings.
whenToUse: Getting information from an outside website (server only).
Sending game stats or error logs to your own web server (server only).
Turning a Luau table into JSON text, or JSON text into a table (works anywhere).
Making a random unique ID for something, like a trade or an item (works anywhere).
kid.where: Get it with `game:GetService("HttpService")`. Web requests (`GetAsync`, `PostAsync`, `RequestAsync`) only work in server Scripts and only when HTTP requests are allowed (Game Settings > Security > Allow HTTP Requests). JSON and GUID functions work on server and client.

terms.HTTP: The language web browsers and websites use to talk. A web address like https://example.com is sent an HTTP request and replies with a response.
terms.client vs server for HttpService: Roblox clients and the Roblox server talk to each other over Roblox's own network connection (that is what RemoteEvents use), NOT over HTTP. HttpService is something different: it lets the SERVER call websites outside Roblox. LocalScripts cannot send web requests.
terms.server: The Roblox computer in charge of one copy of your game. A popular game runs many servers at the same time, each with its own group of players.
terms.client: A player's own device (phone, PC, console). LocalScripts run there.
terms.GET / POST: Two kinds of web request. GET means 'please give me something'. POST means 'here is some data for you'.
terms.JSON: A very common way to write data as text, for example `{"coins":10,"name":"Ava"}`. Websites use it to send data back and forth.
terms.encode / decode: Encode means turn a Luau table into JSON text. Decode means turn JSON text back into a Luau table.
terms.GUID / UUID: A long random ID like `db454790-7563-44ed-ab4b-397ff5df737b`. There are so many possible ones that two will basically never be the same.
terms.secret: A hidden password or API key stored safely in your game's settings. Scripts can use it in requests but cannot print it.
terms.API key: A password a website gives you so it knows the request comes from you.
terms.status code: A number a website replies with. 200 means OK. 404 means not found. 500 means the website had an error.
terms.pcall: Short for 'protected call'. It runs a function and catches errors instead of crashing your script. It returns `true` and the results if it worked, or `false` and the error message if it failed.
terms.async / yield: Functions ending in `Async` talk to other computers over the internet. Your script pauses (yields) until the answer comes back.

examples.title: Ask a website for data (server only)
examples.place: Script in ServerScriptService (turn on Allow HTTP Requests first)
examples.code:
local HttpService = game:GetService("HttpService")

local ok, result = pcall(function()
	return HttpService:GetAsync("https://httpbin.org/get")
end)

if ok then
	-- The reply is JSON text; turn it into a table
	local data = HttpService:JSONDecode(result)
	print("The website saw this address:", data.url)
else
	warn("Request failed: " .. tostring(result))
end
explain: Only a server Script can do this. A LocalScript would get an error.
`GetAsync` sends a GET request and waits for the reply text.
Web requests can fail (site down, internet hiccup, HTTP not allowed), so we use pcall.
`JSONDecode` turns the JSON reply into a Luau table we can read.

examples.title: Turn a table into JSON and back (works anywhere)
explain: `JSONEncode` makes text out of the table.
`JSONDecode` rebuilds a table from the text.
These do not use the internet, so they work even with HTTP requests turned off.

gotchas: Web requests only work from server Scripts. Clients talk to the server with RemoteEvents, not HTTP.
Turn on Game Settings > Security > Allow HTTP Requests, or every request fails.
You cannot call most roblox.com websites with it (only some Open Cloud ones).
There is a limit of about 500 web requests per minute per server. Do not call websites in a fast loop.
Always use pcall: websites can be slow, down, or return errors.
Never put API keys or passwords directly in your scripts. Use secrets with `GetSecret`.
Only call websites you trust.

class/Humanoid.d:
The Humanoid is a special object that gives models the functionality of a character. It grants the model with the ability to physically walk around and interact with various components of a Roblox experience. Humanoids are always parented inside of a Model, and the model is expected to be an assembly of BasePart and Motor6D; the root part of the assembly is expected to be named HumanoidRootPart. It also expects a part named Head to be connected to the character's torso part, either directly or indirectly. By default, there are two official types of character rigs supplied by Roblox, each with their own set of rules:

R6

  • A basic character rig that uses 6 parts for limbs.
  • The Head part must be attached to a part named Torso, or the Humanoid will die immediately.
  • BodyPart appearances are applied using CharacterMesh objects.
  • Certain properties, such as Humanoid.LeftLeg and Humanoid.RightLeg, only work with R6.

R15

  • More complex than R6, but also far more flexible and robust.
  • Uses 15 parts for limbs.
  • The Head part must be attached to a part named UpperTorso or the Humanoid will die immediately.
  • BodyPart appearances have to be assembled directly.
  • Can be dynamically rescaled by using special NumberValue objects parented inside of the Humanoid.
  • The Humanoid will automatically create Vector3Value objects named OriginalSize inside of each limb.
  • If a NumberValue is parented inside of the Humanoid and is named one of the following, it will be used to control the scaling functionality:
  • BodyDepthScale
  • BodyHeightScale
  • BodyWidthScale
  • HeadScale
class/Humanoid.s: A special object that gives models the functionality of a character.

m.d:
AutoJumpEnabled sets whether or not the Humanoid will attempt to automatically jump over an obstacle it is walking towards.

Currently, this property only works when the following conditions are true:

  • The Humanoid's character model is the Player.Character of a Player.
  • The Player in question is using touch controls.

When a player's character spawns, the property's value matches the player's Player.AutoJumpEnabled property - which in turn matches the StarterPlayer.AutoJumpEnabled property.
m.s: Sets whether the character will automatically jump when they hit an obstacle as a player on a mobile device.

kid.simple: If true, a player on a touch screen jumps automatically when walking into a small obstacle. Only works for player characters using touch controls.

m.d: The Humanoid has six child scale values including BodyDepthScale, BodyHeightScale, BodyProportionScale, BodyTypeScale, BodyWidthScale, HeadScale. Changing the value of any of these causes the character's body parts and accessories to change size, but only if AutomaticScalingEnabled is true.
m.s: When Enabled, AutomaticScalingEnabled causes the size of the character to change in response to the values in the humanoid's child scale values changing.

kid.simple: If true, the character's body resizes when you change the scale values inside the Humanoid (like BodyHeightScale or HeadScale). If false, changing those values does nothing.

m.d:
The AutoRotate property describes whether or not the Humanoid will automatically rotate to face in the direction they are moving. When set to true, the character model will gradually turn to face their movement direction as the Humanoid walks around. When set to false, the character model will remain fixated in its current rotation, unless a rotating force is applied to the HumanoidRootPart.

If the character model happens to be the character of a player, then the behavior of the Humanoid's rotation is influenced by the UserGameSetting's RotateType property.

When the AutoRotate property is set to true, the RotateType property has the following effects on the Humanoid's rotation:

RotationType Behavior Context
MovementRelative
CameraRelative Character will rotate to face in the direction of the camera. Player has their camera zoomed into first-person, or they are in shift-lock mode.
m.s: AutoRotate sets whether or not the Humanoid will automatically rotate to face in the direction they are moving in.

kid.simple: If true (normal), the character turns to face the way it's walking. Set false to keep it facing the same way, like when aiming.

m.d: Determines whether the humanoid's joints break when in the HumanoidStateType.Dead state. Defaults to true.
m.s: Determines whether the humanoid's joints break when in the `Enum.HumanoidStateType.Dead` state.

kid.simple: If true (the default), the body falls apart when the character dies. Set to false so it stays in one piece (good for ragdoll effects).

m.d:
The CameraOffset property specifies an offset to the camera's subject position when its Camera.CameraSubject is set to this Humanoid.

The offset is applied in object-space, relative to the orientation of the Humanoid's HumanoidRootPart. For example, an offset Vector3 value of (0, 10, 0) offsets the player's camera to 10 studs above the player's humanoid.
m.s: An offset applied to the Camera's subject position when its CameraSubject is set to this Humanoid.

kid.simple: Moves the camera away from where it normally looks at the character. The offset is measured from the character's own facing, so (0, 2, 0) moves the camera 2 studs up from the normal spot, and (2, 0, 0) moves it 2 studs to the character's right.
kid.example: humanoid.CameraOffset = Vector3.new(0, 2, 0) -- camera looks from 2 studs higher

m.d: This property selects the HumanoidCollisionType for R15 and Rthro non-player characters.
m.s: Selects the `Enum.HumanoidCollisionType` for R15 and Rthro non-player characters.
m.dep: Deprecated.

kid.simple: Old — no longer needed; Roblox handles character collisions for you.

m.d:
The DisplayDistanceType property controls the distance behavior of the humanoid's name and health display. This property is set using the HumanoidDisplayDistanceType enum with three available values, each with their own set of rules:

  • When set to Viewer, the humanoid sees the name/health of other humanoids within range of its own NameDisplayDistance and HealthDisplayDistance.
  • When set to Subject, the humanoid takes full control over its own name and health display through its NameDisplayDistance and HealthDisplayDistance values.
  • When set to None, the humanoid's name and health bar do not appear under any circumstances.

See Character Name/Health Display for an in-depth guide on controlling the appearance of character names and health bars.
m.s: Controls the distance behavior of the humanoid's name and health display.

kid.simple: Controls who decides when this character's name and health bar show. Viewer: each viewer's own distance settings decide. Subject: this Humanoid's NameDisplayDistance and HealthDisplayDistance decide. None: never show them.
kid.example: humanoid.DisplayDistanceType = Enum.HumanoidDisplayDistanceType.None -- hide name and health bar

m.d:
DisplayName is a property that determines the Humanoid's name display when visible. By default, a new Humanoid will have the value of an empty string. If DisplayName is an empty string, the humanoid's name display will default to the humanoid's parent's name property.

Player Character Loading

When players load their character, either automatically or through the use of LoadCharacterAsync(), the Humanoid that is created by the engine will have its DisplayName property set to the player's DisplayName property.

StarterCharacter and StarterHumanoid

When a Humanoid named StarterHumanoid is parented to StarterPlayer, or when a Humanoid is present in a Model named StarterCharacter, the DisplayName property will be respected when Characters are loaded by Players in the game. The engine will only override the DisplayName property of the Humanoid with the DisplayName property of the player if the Humanoid.DisplayName of StarterHumanoid is an empty string.
m.s: Sets the text of a Humanoid, displayed above their head.

kid.simple: The text shown above the character's head. If empty, the Model's name is shown. For players it is set to their DisplayName when they spawn.

m.d:
Used to disable the internal physics and state machine of the Humanoid.

What does turning this off do?

  • No forces - The humanoid will not apply forces to any of its parts. The humanoid will not move the character in any way.
  • No sensors - The humanoid will not run any spatial queries to detect floors, ladders, or other obstacles (such as auto-jump).
  • No collision changes - The humanoid will not alter the collision state of any of the character parts. By default, only the torso and head have Part.CanCollide enabled.
  • No state transitions or replication - The humanoid will not automatically update its state. You can still set humanoid state with a script, but it will not automatically replicate.

What does turning this off not do?

  • State events - If manually setting humanoid states, the events for each of the humanoid's states and StateChanged will still fire, which means the Animate script will still receive them and animate the character based on its current humanoid state.
  • Appearance - HumanoidDescription, clothes, accessories and other humanoid rendering behavior.
  • Camera and player scripts - The humanoid is still linked to Players and camera scripts, which ensures the camera will continue to follow the Humanoid.RootPart.
  • Player input handling - The Humanoid.MoveDirection property will still be updated via the Humanoid:Move() function and PlayerScripts for input.
m.s: Used to disable the internal physics and state machine of the Humanoid.

kid.simple: If set to false, the Humanoid stops doing its own physics: no walking forces, no floor checks, no automatic state changes. Only for advanced custom character controllers.

m.d:
This is a read-only property that describes the Material the Humanoid is currently standing on. It works with both regular Parts and Terrain voxels.

The code sample below demonstrates how to listen to when this property changes using Object:GetPropertyChangedSignal(). When the material the humanoid is standing on changes, it will print a message indicating the new material being stood on.

local Humanoid = route.to.humanoid

Humanoid:GetPropertyChangedSignal("FloorMaterial"):Connect(function()
    print("New value for FloorMaterial: " .. tostring(Humanoid.FloorMaterial))
end)

Caveats

  • When the Humanoid is not standing on a floor, the value of this property will be set to Air.
  • This occurs because Enum properties cannot have an empty value.
  • This can cause some confusion if a part has its material is set to Air, though in practice, parts are not supposed to use that material in the first place.
  • The character model of the Humanoid must be able to collide with the floor, or else it will not be detected.
  • You cannot test if the Humanoid is swimming with this property. You should instead use its Humanoid:GetState() function.
m.s: Describes the `Enum.Material` that the `Class.Humanoid` is currently standing on. If the `Class.Humanoid` isn't standing on anything, the value of this property will be _Air_.

kid.simple: Read-only. The material the character is standing on, like Grass or Ice. It's Air when the character is in the air.
kid.example:
humanoid:GetPropertyChangedSignal("FloorMaterial"):Connect(function()
    if humanoid.FloorMaterial == Enum.Material.Ice then
        print("Slippery!")
    end
end)

m.d:
This property represents the current health of the Humanoid. The value is restricted to the range between 0 and MaxHealth. If the humanoid is dead, this property is continually set to 0.

Note that the TakeDamage() function may be used to subtract from Health instead of setting the property directly.

Health Regeneration

By default, a passive health regeneration script is automatically inserted into humanoids. This causes non-dead player characters to regenerate 1% of MaxHealth each second. To disable this regeneration behavior, add an empty Script named Health to StarterCharacterScripts.

Health Bar Display

When Health is less than MaxHealth, a health bar is displayed in-experience. The display behavior of the health bar is dependent on the HealthDisplayDistance and HealthDisplayType.

See Character Name/Health Display for an in-depth guide on controlling the appearance of character names and health bars.

Death

When the value of the character's health reaches 0, the Humanoid automatically transitions to the HumanoidStateType.Dead state. In this state, Health is locked to 0; however, there is no error or warning for setting the Health of a dead humanoid to a positive nonzero value.
m.s: Describes the current health of the Humanoid on the range [0, `Class.Humanoid.MaxHealth`].

kid.simple: How much life the character has, from 0 up to MaxHealth. At 0 the character dies. By default players slowly heal 1% of MaxHealth every second.
kid.example:
humanoid.Health = humanoid.MaxHealth -- full heal
humanoid.Health = 0 -- defeat instantly
kid.gotcha: To stop automatic healing, put an empty Script named Health in StarterCharacterScripts.

m.d:
This property is a number used in conjunction with the DisplayDistanceType property to control the distance from which a humanoid's health bar can be seen.

See Character Name/Health Display for an in-depth guide on controlling the appearance of character names and health bars.
m.s: Used in conjunction with the `Class.Humanoid.DisplayDistanceType|DisplayDistanceType` property to control the distance from which a humanoid's health bar can be seen.

kid.simple: Works with DisplayDistanceType: how close (in studs) you must be to see a health bar.

m.d:
This property controls when a humanoid's health bar is allowed to be displayed. By default, this property is set to DisplayWhenDamaged, which makes the health bar only display when a humanoid's Health is less than its MaxHealth. It can also be set to AlwaysOn, which makes the health bar always display, or AlwaysOff, which prevents it from ever displaying.

Note that this property functions independently of the humanoid's HealthDisplayDistance property which is responsible for making the health bar fade out at certain distances. If Humanoid.HealthDisplayType|HealthDisplayType is set to AlwaysOn, it will still fade out depending the how HealthDisplayDistance is configured.

See Character Name/Health Display for an in-depth guide on controlling the appearance of character names and health bars.
m.s: Controls when the humanoid's health bar is allowed to be displayed.

kid.simple: When the health bar may show: DisplayWhenDamaged (default, only when hurt), AlwaysOn, or AlwaysOff.

m.d:
Determines the distance (in studs) off the ground the RootPart should be when the humanoid is standing. The RigType influences the way this property behaves.

For R15 rigs, a suitable hip height is preset to ensure the height of the RootPart is correct. The height of the legs is not used. The overall height of the humanoid can be described in the following formula:

Height = (0.5 * RootPart.Size.Y) + HipHeight

For R6 rigs, HipHeight instead describes a relative offset. The overall height of the humanoid can be described in the following formula:

Height = LeftLeg.Size.Y + (0.5 * RootPart.Size.Y) + HipHeight
m.s: Determines the distance off the ground the `Class.Humanoid.RootPart` should be.

kid.simple: How high (in studs) the HumanoidRootPart floats above the ground when standing. Bigger numbers make the character stand taller (or hover). R15 characters set this for you.
kid.example: humanoid.HipHeight = 5 -- float higher off the ground

m.d: If true, the Humanoid jumps with an upwards force equal to the value of Humanoid.JumpPower or the height of Humanoid.JumpHeight, depending on the value of Humanoid.UseJumpPower.
m.s: If `true`, the `Class.Humanoid` jumps with an upwards force.

kid.simple: Set it to true to make the character jump once (if it is standing on something).

m.d:
Provides control over the height a Humanoid jumps, in studs. The starting value of this property is determined by the value of StarterPlayer.CharacterJumpHeight which defaults to 7.2.

Although setting this property to 0 will effectively prevent the humanoid from jumping, it's recommended to disable jumping by disabling the HumanoidStateType.Jumping state through Humanoid:SetStateEnabled().

This property is only visible in the Properties window if Humanoid.UseJumpPower is set to false, as it is not relevant otherwise (instead, Humanoid.JumpPower is used).
m.s: Provides control over the height that the `Class.Humanoid` jumps to.

kid.simple: How high the character jumps, in studs (default 7.2). Only used when UseJumpPower is false.

m.d:
Determines how much upwards force is applied to the Humanoid when jumping. The starting value of this property is determined by the value of StarterPlayer.CharacterJumpPower which defaults to 50 and is constrained between 0 and 1000. Note that jumps are also influenced by the Workspace.Gravity property which determines the acceleration due to gravity.

Although setting this property to 0 will effectively prevent the humanoid from jumping, it's recommended to disable jumping by disabling the HumanoidStateType.Jumping state through Humanoid:SetStateEnabled().

This property is only visible in the Properties window if Humanoid.UseJumpPower is set to true, as it is not relevant otherwise (instead, Humanoid.JumpHeight is used).
m.s: Determines how much upwards force is applied to the `Class.Humanoid` when jumping.

kid.simple: How strong the upward push is when jumping (default 50). Only used when UseJumpPower is true. Gravity also affects how high you go.
kid.gotcha: To stop jumping completely, use humanoid:SetStateEnabled(Enum.HumanoidStateType.Jumping, false) instead of setting this to 0.

m.d: A reference to the humanoid's Left Leg part. The value of this property will always be nil if the humanoid's RigType is set to R15.
m.s: A reference to the humanoid's _Left Leg_ part.
m.dep: This instance only works with the old R6 rig. It will not work with the R15 rig and should not be used in new work not using the R6 rig.

kid.simple: Old — only worked with R6. Use character:FindFirstChild("Left Leg") or Humanoid:GetBodyPartR15 instead.

m.d:
The maximum value of a humanoid's Health.

The value of this property is used alongside the Health property to size the default health bar display. When a humanoid's Health reaches MaxHealth, its health bar may not be displayed, depending on its HealthDisplayType property.
m.s: The maximum value of a humanoid's `Class.Humanoid.Health|Health`.

kid.simple: The most health the character can have (default 100). Health can't go above it.

m.dep: This deprecated property is a variant of Humanoid.MaxHealth which should be used instead.

kid.simple: Old — use Humanoid.MaxHealth instead.

m.d:
This property determines the maximum slope angle that a humanoid can climb. If the angle of a slope is greater than a humanoid's MaxSlopeAngle, they will slide down the slope.

When a character spawns, this property is set according to the value of StarterPlayer.CharacterMaxSlopeAngle.

The value of this property is constrained to values between 0° and 89°. It defaults to 89°, so humanoids can climb pretty much any slope they want by default.
m.s: The maximum slope angle that a humanoid can walk on without slipping.

kid.simple: The steepest slope (in degrees, 0 to 89) the character can walk up. Steeper slopes make it slide down. Default 89, so almost anything.

m.d:
MoveDirection is a read-only property that describes the direction a Humanoid is walking in, as a unit vector or zero length vector. The direction is described in world space.

Because this property is read-only, it cannot be set by a Script or LocalScript.
m.s: Describes the direction that the `Class.Humanoid` is walking in.

kid.simple: Read-only. Which way the character is trying to walk, as a direction in world space (length 1), or (0, 0, 0) when standing still.
kid.example:
if humanoid.MoveDirection.Magnitude > 0 then
    print("Walking") -- Magnitude is the length of the direction
end

m.d:
The NameDisplayDistance property is a number used in conjunction with the Humanoid.DisplayDistanceType property to control the distance from which a humanoid's name can be seen.

See Character Name/Health Display for an in-depth guide on controlling the appearance of character names and health bars.
m.s: Used in conjunction with the `Class.Humanoid.DisplayDistanceType` property to control the distance from which a humanoid's name can be seen.

kid.simple: Works with DisplayDistanceType: how close (in studs) you must be to see a name.

m.d:
Controls whether a humanoid's name and health bar can be seen behind walls or other objects. This property is a NameOcclusion value and can be configured to occlude all names, enemy names, or disable occlusion entirely.

In cases where the LocalPlayer has no Humanoid associated with it, this property instead applies to the subject Humanoid.

See Character Name/Health Display for an in-depth guide on controlling the appearance of character names and health bars.
m.s: Controls whether a humanoid's name and health bar can be seen behind walls or other objects.

kid.simple: Whether names and health bars can be seen through walls. You can hide all names behind walls, hide only enemies' names, or never hide them.

m.d: Determines whether the Humanoid is currently in the HumanoidStateType.PlatformStanding state. When true, the Humanoid is in a state where it is free-falling and cannot move. This state behaves similar to sitting, except that jumping does not free the humanoid from the state.
m.s: Determines whether the `Class.Humanoid` is currently in the `Enum.HumanoidStateType.PlatformStanding` state.

kid.simple: If true, the character goes limp and can't move by itself, a bit like sitting but jumping won't get it out. Set back to false to let it move again.

m.d: Allows developers to disable the behavior where a player Character|character dies if the Neck Motor6D is removed or disconnected even momentarily. This property defaults to true.
m.s: Allows developers to disable the behavior where a player `Character|character` dies if the Neck `Class.Motor6D` is removed or disconnected even momentarily.

kid.simple: If true (default), the character dies if its neck joint is removed, even for a moment. Set false if your game swaps heads or rebuilds the body.

m.d: A reference to the humanoid's Right Leg part. The value of this property will always be nil if the humanoid's RigType is set to R15.
m.s: A reference to the humanoid's _Right Leg_ part.
m.dep: This instance only works with the old R6 rig. It will not work with the R15 rig and should not be used in new work not using the R6 rig.

kid.simple: Old — only worked with R6. Use character:FindFirstChild("Right Leg") or Humanoid:GetBodyPartR15 instead.

m.d:
RigType describes whether a Humanoid is utilizing the legacy R6 character rig, or the newer R15 character rig.

The R6 rig uses 6 visible Parts while the R15 rig uses 15 visible Parts. R15 rigs have more joints than R6 rigs, making them much more versatile when being animated.

Note that if this property is set incorrectly, the Humanoid will not function correctly. For example, if a R15 humanoid's RigType is set to R6, the Humanoid will die as there is no BasePart called Torso connected to a BasePart called Head.
m.s: Describes whether this `Class.Humanoid` is utilizing the legacy R6 character rig, or the new R15 character rig.

kid.simple: Says whether the character is R6 (6 body parts) or R15 (15 body parts).
kid.example:
if humanoid.RigType == Enum.HumanoidRigType.R15 then
    print("Modern R15 body")
end
kid.gotcha: Setting the wrong rig type kills the Humanoid, because it can't find the body parts it expects.

m.d:
A reference to the humanoid's HumanoidRootPart object. The HumanoidRootPart is required for all assemblies that include a Humanoid and is the primary driving part of the Humanoid that controls a humanoid's movement through the 3D world. This part is normally invisible and typically resides in the local origin center of the character model.

The HumanoidRootPart is included in all platform-wide avatar characters, and automatically created when a character model is imported into Studio. It's possible to manually add a HumanoidRootPart to a model by adding a Part named HumanoidRootPart and ensuring it's the root part of the assembly.

Use this property to reference the specific HumanoidRootPart without searching the model hierarchy. You can get or set the CFrame of this part to change position or reorient the entire character model.

For R15 or higher-fidelity characters, the Model.PrimaryPart of the Player.Character model is also set to HumanoidRootPart.

While R6 characters also include a HumanoidRootPart, the R6 characters, Model.PrimaryPart is set to the Head part.
m.s: A reference to the humanoid's `HumanoidRootPart` object.

kid.simple: Read-only shortcut to the character's HumanoidRootPart, the invisible part in the middle that everything follows. Move it to move the whole character.
kid.example:
local root = humanoid.RootPart
if root then
    print("Character is at " .. tostring(root.Position))
end

m.d:
SeatPart is a reference to the seat that a Humanoid is currently sitting in, if any. The value of this property can be either a Seat, or a VehicleSeat. It will be nil if the Humanoid is not currently sitting in a seat.

Note:

  • For a bool describing if the Humanoid is currently sitting or not, see Humanoid.Sit
m.s: A reference to the seat that a `Class.Humanoid` is currently sitting in, if any.

kid.simple: Read-only. The Seat or VehicleSeat the character is sitting in, or nil if it isn't sitting.
kid.example:
if humanoid.SeatPart then
    print("Sitting in " .. humanoid.SeatPart.Name)
end

m.d:
The Sit property is a boolean that indicates whether the Humanoid is currently sitting. Humanoids can be forced into a sitting state by setting this property's value to true. If the Humanoid isn't attached to a seat while in its sitting state, it will trip over with no collision in its legs. A Humanoid can escape from the sitting state by jumping.

Note:

  • The Seat or VehicleSeat the Humanoid is sitting on can be obtained using the Humanoid.SeatPart property
  • It is possible to detect when a Humanoid sits by connecting to the Humanoid.Seated event.
m.s: Describes whether the `Class.Humanoid` is currently sitting.

kid.simple: True if the character is sitting. Set it to true to force it to sit. Jumping gets it back up.

m.d:
Do not use This property only works with Experimental Mode enabled, which has been entirely discontinued.

This property describes a 3D position in space where the Player controlling this Humanoid last clicked with a Tool equipped.

This property is primarily used by classic tools to determine what a humanoid is targeting when they activate a tool. If you give an NPC a classic rocket launcher, set their TargetPoint, and then call the tool's Tool:Activate() function, you can make the NPC fire a rocket at the target point.
m.s: Describes the 3D position where the `Class.Player` controlling the `Class.Humanoid` last clicked in the world while using a `Class.Tool`.

kid.simple: Don't use. It only worked in a discontinued mode. It was the spot a player last clicked with a tool.

m.d: A reference to a humanoid's root driving part. Contrary to the name of this property, it will only point to the Torso part if a humanoid doesn't have a HumanoidRootPart.
m.s: A reference to a humanoid's root driving part.
m.dep: This instance only works with the old R6 rig. It will not work with the R15 rig and should not be used in new work not using the R6 rig.

kid.simple: Old — only worked with R6. Use Humanoid.RootPart instead.

m.d:
When a character spawns, this property is set according to the value of StarterPlayer.CharacterUseJumpPower, which defaults to true.

When jumping, with this set to false, the Humanoid.JumpHeight value is used to ensure the humanoid jumps to that height. With this set to true, the Humanoid.JumpPower value is used to apply an upward force.
m.s: Determines whether the `Class.Humanoid.JumpHeight|JumpHeight` (false) or `Class.Humanoid.JumpPower` (true) property is used.

kid.simple: Picks which jump setting is used: true uses JumpPower (a push strength), false uses JumpHeight (a height in studs). It starts from StarterPlayer.CharacterUseJumpPower.
kid.example: humanoid.UseJumpPower = false -- now JumpHeight is used

m.d:
This property describes how quickly the Humanoid is able to walk, in studs per second. It defaults to the value of StarterPlayer.CharacterWalkSpeed (16), meaning a player character can move 16 studs in any direction each second.

Notes

  • When controlled on a mobile device or a gamepad, a humanoid can walk slower than its WalkSpeed if the controlling thumbstick is moved just a gradual degree from center.
  • You can freeze a humanoid in place by setting WalkSpeed to 0, effectively preventing the controlling player from moving it through the default movement mechanisms. Note, however, that WalkSpeed is a client‑replicated property which can be modified locally, so it should not be used as a security mechanism or as the sole method for preventing humanoid movement.
  • The default animation script scales a humanoid's movement animations based on how fast it is moving relative to the default speed of 16 studs/second.
  • The speed at which the Humanoid is currently walking can be obtained using the Running event.
m.s: Describes the humanoid's maximum movement speed in studs per second.

kid.simple: How fast the character walks, in studs per second. The default is 16, so it covers 16 studs every second. 0 freezes it in place.
kid.example: humanoid.WalkSpeed = 32 -- twice as fast as normal
kid.gotcha: Players can change this on their own device, so don't rely on it to stop cheaters.

m.d:
WalkToPart is a reference to a BasePart that the humanoid is trying to reach, after having been prompted to do so via the MoveTo() method.

When WalkToPart is set and a humanoid is actively trying to reach the part, it will keep updating its Vector3 goal to be the position of the part, plus the WalkToPoint translated in object space relative to the rotation of the part. This can be described in Luau as:

goal = humanoid.WalkToPart.CFrame:PointToObjectSpace(humanoid.WalkToPoint)

Note that simply setting the value of WalkToPart is not sufficient to make a humanoid start "following" a part. Call MoveTo() to initiate movement.
m.s: A reference to a part whose position is trying to be reached by a humanoid.

kid.simple: The part the Humanoid is walking toward after MoveTo was given a part. If the part moves, the goal moves with it. Setting this alone doesn't start walking; call MoveTo.

m.d:
WalkToPoint describes the 3D position in space that a humanoid is trying to reach, after having been prompted to do so via the MoveTo() method.

If a humanoid's WalkToPart is set, the goal is set by transforming WalkToPoint relative to the part's position and rotation. Otherwise, the humanoid will try to reach the 3D position specified by WalkToPoint directly.

Note that simply setting the value of WalkToPoint is not sufficient to make a humanoid start moving toward a point. Call MoveTo() to initiate movement.
m.s: The position that a humanoid is trying to reach, after a call to `Class.Humanoid:MoveTo()` is made.

kid.simple: The position the Humanoid is walking to after MoveTo. If WalkToPart is set, this point is measured from that part instead of from the world center. Setting it alone doesn't start walking; call MoveTo.

m.d:
This method attaches the specified Accessory to the humanoid's parent.

When this method is called, an Accessory is attached to the character by searching for an Attachment in the humanoid's parent that shares the same name as an Attachment in the accessory's Handle Part. If one is found, the Handle part will be connected to the parent of the Attachment using a Weld, and the weld will be configured so the Attachments occupy the same space.

If the required Attachment can not be found, then the Accessory will remain parented to the humanoid's parent but it will be unattached.

Typically, accessory welds are created on the server, but they can be created on the client under certain circumstances. In these situations, client-sided calls to AddAccessory() may not always produce the desired behavior and you can use BuildRigFromAttachments() to force the expected weld creation.
m.s: Attaches the specified `Class.Accessory` to the humanoid's parent.

p.s: The Accessory to be attached.

kid.simple: Puts an Accessory (like a hat) on the character. It finds an Attachment on the body with the same name as the one in the accessory's Handle (for example HatAttachment) and welds it there.
kid.gotcha: If no matching Attachment is found, the accessory is added but just falls off.

This yielding method makes the character's look match that of the passed in HumanoidDescription. A copy of the passed HumanoidDescription is cached as the HumanoidDescription for the Humanoid.

This method is optimized through making the assumption that only this method is used to change the appearance of the character, and no changes are made through other means between calls. If changes are made to the character between calls, then this method may not make the character reflect the passed in HumanoidDescription accurately.

This method has been superseded by ApplyDescriptionAsync(), which should be used for all new work.

The asset type verification mode.

If changes are made to the character between calls, then this method may not make the character reflect the passed in HumanoidDescription accurately. If you want to use this method in conjunction with other means of updating the character, Humanoid:ApplyDescriptionResetAsync() will always ensure the character reflects the passed in HumanoidDescription.

See Also

  • Humanoid:GetAppliedDescription() which returns the HumanoidDescription currently applied to the humanoid.
  • Players:GetHumanoidDescriptionFromUserIdAsync() which returns a HumanoidDescription describing the avatar for the passed in user.
  • Players:GetHumanoidDescriptionFromOutfitIdAsync() which returns a HumanoidDescription whose parameters are initialized to match that of the passed in server-side outfit asset.
  • Player:LoadCharacterWithHumanoidDescriptionAsync() which spawns a player with the look from the passed in HumanoidDescription.
m.s: Makes the character's look match that of the passed in `Class.HumanoidDescription`. If `HumanoidDescription.UseAvatarSettings` is true, the Avatar Settings for the experience will also be applied to the character.

p.s: The HumanoidDescription instance which you want to set the character to match.
The asset type verification mode.

kid.simple: Changes the character's whole look (clothes, accessories, body colors, sizes, animations) to match a HumanoidDescription. It waits until the change is finished.
kid.example:
-- Script (server): make a character 20% taller
local description = humanoid:GetAppliedDescription() -- copy of current look
description.HeightScale = 1.2
humanoid:ApplyDescriptionAsync(description)
kid.gotcha: Only call it on the server. If other scripts changed the character in other ways, use ApplyDescriptionResetAsync instead.

This is in contrast to Humanoid:ApplyDescription() which is optimized and may incorrectly apply a HumanoidDescription if the character has been changed by means other than through the HumanoidDescription system.
